analysis.one_liner: Exempts mortgage servicers from debt-collector disclosure rules when collecting defaulted home loans.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill by voice vote on October 7, 2002, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, a company that takes over servicing on mortgage loans that are already behind on payments is treated as a debt collector and must follow the law's rules, including telling borrowers that the message is from a debt collector and how to dispute the debt. This bill would carve out an exemption for mortgage servicers whose main business is servicing current loans, covering collection activity on federally related first-lien mortgages that were in default when the servicer took them over [S2][S3]. The House passed it quickly with no recorded vote; the Senate never acted [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Mortgage servicers — companies that collect payments and handle escrow on home loans — gain if the bill passes. When they take over servicing of loans already in default, they would no longer have to include the debt-collector disclosure on their collection communications [S3]. Supporters argued this clarified the law rather than weakening it, since servicing current loans, not collecting delinquent debts, is these companies' primary function [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill inserts a new section into the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act exempting a 'covered mortgage servicer' — a debt collector whose primary function is servicing current federally related first-lien mortgages — from section 807(11) when collecting debts on mortgages that were already in default when the servicer became responsible for them [S3].

Section 807(11) is the provision that requires a collector to disclose that a communication is from a debt collector and to state that the borrower can dispute the debt; the exemption removes that disclosure requirement for these servicers [S3].
The exemption covers servicers who become responsible for the loans 'by assignment, sale or transfer,' meaning servicing rights sold between companies on defaulted loans are squarely covered [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Homeowners whose mortgages were already in default when servicing was transferred would receive collection communications without the standard notice that the contact is from a debt collector or how to dispute the debt. The bill passed the House with no roll-call vote, so no individual member is on record on the merits [S5].
analysis.who_pays_short: Homeowners in default on transferred mortgages

drawbacks.text: The bill removes a consumer protection precisely where borrowers are most vulnerable: a homeowner behind on a mortgage whose servicing was just sold would no longer get the notice that a communication is an attempt to collect a debt or how to dispute it [S3].
The House passed the bill under a procedure used for non-controversial bills, by voice vote, so no member's position was recorded and there was no recorded debate vote [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The practical stakes are modest: this is a narrow compliance carve-out for one disclosure requirement affecting servicers who inherit already-defaulted first-lien mortgages, not a broad rewrite of collection law. Still, the cost falls entirely on defaulted borrowers, who lose a disclosure that helps them recognize and contest collection activity, while the benefit is a convenience for servicers. A fairer design could have required servicers to give equivalent information without the debt-collector label.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it by voice vote on a suspension motion in October 2002, but the Senate never brought it up before that Congress ended in January 2003, so the bill died without becoming law.

narrative.text: Rep. Edward Royce (R-CA) introduced the Mortgage Servicing Clarification Act on January 3, 2001, the first day of the 107th Congress, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee [S1][S5].
On March 2, 2001, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Financial Institutions and Consumer Credit, where it sat for over a year and a half [S5].

On October 7, 2002, Royce moved to suspend the rules and pass the bill as amended — a procedure reserved for non-controversial bills that requires a two-thirds majority — and the House agreed to it by voice vote, with 40 minutes of debate [S5].
The Senate received the bill on October 8, 2002, the day after House passage, but took no further action before the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, homeowners facing collection on defaulted mortgages whose servicing was transferred kept the debt-collector disclosure protections the bill would have lifted. Mortgage servicers did not get the compliance relief they sought.

for.name: Rep. Edward Royce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 107th Congress and, 21 months later, moved to suspend the rules and pass it as amended, bringing it to the House floor.

for.name: 8 of 208 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: The House of Representatives
for.what_they_did: Agreed to the bill by voice vote under suspension of the rules on October 7, 2002, with no recorded vote.

against.name: Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 8, 2002 and never voted on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
against.what_they_did: Controlled the Senate floor calendar in the final months of the 107th Congress and did not bring the bill to the floor for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill drew cosponsors from both parties (8 Democrats and 4 Republicans) and passed the House on a voice vote with no recorded opposition; the Senate never took a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill exempts servicers whose primary business is servicing current first-lien mortgages from the FDCPA debt-collector disclosure when collecting on mortgages already in default at the time servicing was transferred [S3]. The relief is theirs; the reduced disclosure falls on borrowers behind on their homes.

Ordinary debt collectors buying defaulted loans still fall fully under the FDCPA; only servicers of current first-lien mortgage portfolios get the carve-out, so the bill creates a narrower disclosure obligation for some collectors of defaulted home debt than for others [S3].
